gloss_terse: Oholibamah — a wife of Esau and an Edomite clan chief, meaning 'tent of the high place'
gloss_readable: Oholibamah (meaning 'tent of the high place') appears exclusively in the Esau genealogies of Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 1. She is identified as the daughter of Anah and wife of Esau, through whom several Edomite clans traced their lineage. The name may also designate an Edomite chief or clan. Cross-language renderings are remarkably consistent — English 'Oholibamah,' Spanish 'Oholibama,' French and German similarly preserving the Hebrew form — reflecting the standard treatment of proper names in translation.

senses.1: The personal and clan name Oholibamah (אָהֳלִיבָמָה), etymologically 'tent of the high place,' designating Esau's wife (daughter of Anah, granddaughter of Zibeon the Hivite) and the Edomite clan descending from her. All eight occurrences cluster in Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 1:52, the Edomite genealogical registers. Translations across languages uniformly transliterate the name with minimal variation, confirming a single referent throughout.

gloss_terse: Onan — second son of Judah, whose name means 'vigorous' or 'strong'
gloss_readable: Onan was the second son of Judah and his Canaanite wife, best known from the narrative in Genesis 38 where he refused to fulfill the duty of levirate marriage for his deceased brother Er. His name, meaning 'vigorous,' appears eight times across Genesis, Numbers, and 1 Chronicles. The multilingual evidence — Hindi ओनान, Spanish Onán, French and German Onan — shows uniform transliteration, as expected for a personal name with no semantic ambiguity in context.

senses.1: The proper masculine name Onan (אוֹנָן, 'vigorous'), referring to Judah's second son by his Canaanite wife (Gen 38:4). He is remembered for his refusal to raise offspring for his brother Er, resulting in divine judgment (Gen 38:8–10). Later genealogical lists in Genesis 46:12, Numbers 26:19, and 1 Chronicles 2:3 record his name in the tribal registers of Judah. All languages transliterate consistently, confirming a single, unambiguous referent.

gloss_terse: Uri — a Hebrew proper name meaning 'fiery,' borne by three distinct men in the Old Testament
gloss_readable: Uri (meaning 'fiery,' possibly a shortened form of Uriah) is borne by at least three individuals in Scripture: the father of Bezalel, chief artisan of the tabernacle (Exod 31:2; 35:30; 38:22); a temple porter in Ezra's time (Ezra 10:24); and the father of one of Solomon's district governors (1 Kgs 4:19). Despite referring to different people, translations consistently render the name as a simple transliteration — English and Spanish 'Uri,' French and German the same — reflecting its transparent phonology.

senses.1: The proper masculine name Uri (אוּרִי, 'fiery,' or a contraction of Uriah), applied to three distinct individuals: (a) a prince of Judah, father of Bezalel the tabernacle craftsman (Exod 31:2; 1 Chr 2:20; 2 Chr 1:5); (b) a gatekeeper who had married a foreign wife (Ezra 10:24); and (c) the father of Geber, one of Solomon's regional officers (1 Kgs 4:19). All eight occurrences are rendered uniformly across languages as a straightforward transliteration.

gloss_terse: A hind or doe (female deer), used in poetry as a figure of grace, swiftness, and sure-footedness
gloss_readable: This feminine noun designates the hind or doe — the female deer — and appears almost exclusively in poetic and wisdom literature. Naphtali is compared to a doe set free giving beautiful words (Gen 49:21), and God is praised for making feet swift and sure like those of a hind (2 Sam 22:34; Ps 18:33; Hab 3:19). The Song of Songs adjures by the 'does of the field' (Song 2:7; 3:5). Spanish 'cierva,' French 'biche,' and German 'Hirschkuh' all confirm the consistent zoological identification across traditions.

senses.1: The feminine noun אַיָּלָה, denoting a female deer (hind, doe), used across poetic, wisdom, and prophetic contexts as a symbol of grace and agility. In Genesis 49:21, Naphtali is likened to a doe let loose; in 2 Samuel 22:34, Psalm 18:33, and Habakkuk 3:19, God makes the psalmist's feet like those of a hind — swift and sure-footed on high places. Job 39:1 and Psalm 29:9 depict the doe calving. Song of Songs 2:7 and 3:5 invoke the 'does of the field' in an adjuration formula. Multilingual glosses — Spanish 'cierva,' French 'biche,' German 'Hirschkuh/Gazelle' — uniformly identify the animal as a female cervid.

gloss_terse: Ethan — a proper name meaning 'enduring,' especially Ethan the Ezrahite, famed for wisdom
gloss_readable: Ethan (meaning 'enduring' or 'permanent') is best known as Ethan the Ezrahite, whose wisdom was surpassed only by Solomon's (1 Kgs 4:31), and to whom Psalm 89 is attributed in its superscription. He appears in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as a son of Zerah (1 Chr 2:6) and as a Levitical singer alongside Heman and Asaph (1 Chr 6:42–44; 15:17, 19). French 'Ethan,' Spanish 'Etán,' and German 'Etan' all preserve the name faithfully across translation traditions.

senses.1: The proper masculine name Ethan (אֵיתָן as personal name, distinct from the common adjective meaning 'enduring'), referring primarily to Ethan the Ezrahite, celebrated for wisdom that rivaled Solomon's (1 Kgs 4:31) and credited in the superscription of Psalm 89. In the Chronicler's genealogies he is listed among the sons of Zerah (1 Chr 2:6, 8) and identified as a Levitical singer appointed alongside Heman and Asaph (1 Chr 6:42, 44; 15:17, 19). Translations uniformly transliterate: French 'Ethan,' Spanish 'Etán/Etan,' German 'Etan.'

gloss_terse: Cruel, fierce, merciless — describing persons or forces that act with savage harshness
gloss_readable: This adjective paints a vivid picture of ruthless severity. Proverbs warns that even the mercies of the wicked are cruel (12:10) and that a cruel messenger will be sent against the rebel (17:11). Jeremiah describes enemy armies as cruel and without compassion (6:23; 50:42). Isaiah uses it of the terrible day of the LORD (13:9). The Spanish 'cruel,' French 'cruel,' and English 'cruel' all converge on the same stark meaning, while the German 'grausam' (grim, gruesome) adds a visceral overtone.

senses.1: The adjective אַכְזָרִי describing a person, force, or quality as cruel, fierce, or merciless. In wisdom literature it characterizes harsh taskmasters (Prov 5:9 'the cruel one'), the false compassion of the wicked (Prov 12:10), and the merciless messenger sent against rebels (Prov 17:11). Prophetically, Jeremiah applies it to the invading Babylonians — a people 'cruel and without mercy' (Jer 6:23; 50:42) — while Isaiah deploys it eschatologically for the day of the LORD (Isa 13:9). Cross-linguistic evidence is strikingly uniform: Spanish, French, and English all render 'cruel,' German 'grausam,' confirming the core semantic of savage, pitiless harshness.

gloss_terse: Oak tree (genus Quercus), a symbol of strength, majesty, and endurance in biblical imagery
gloss_readable: The oak (אַלּוֹן) figures prominently in both narrative and prophetic poetry. It marks the burial site of Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, beneath the 'oak of weeping' at Bethel (Gen 35:8). The prophets invoke it as a symbol of towering strength — the oaks of Bashan represent pride before God's judgment (Isa 2:13; Zech 11:2) — and Hosea condemns idolatrous worship under oaks (Hos 4:13). Spanish 'encina,' French 'chene,' and the Septuagint's drys all confirm identification with the oak genus rather than the terebinth.

senses.1: The masculine noun אַלּוֹן designating the oak tree (Quercus), distinct from the terebinth (אֵלָה) though sometimes confused in older translations. It appears in narrative as a memorial marker — Deborah's burial oak at Bethel (Gen 35:8, 'the oak of weeping'). Prophetically it symbolizes towering strength and pride: the 'oaks of Bashan' represent what God will bring low (Isa 2:13; Zech 11:2), Amos compares the Amorites' height to oaks (Amos 2:9), and Hosea condemns illicit worship under oaks (Hos 4:13). It also serves as timber for shipbuilding (Ezek 27:6) and idol-making (Isa 44:14). Spanish 'encina' and German 'Eiche' confirm the oak identification.

gloss_terse: Do not destroy — Hifil jussive of שָׁחַת, a Psalm superscription formula ('Al-Tashcheth')
gloss_readable: This form is the negated Hifil jussive of שָׁחַת ('to destroy, ruin'), appearing in the liturgical superscription אַל־תַּשְׁחֵת ('Do not destroy') found in Psalms 57, 58, 59, and 75. The phrase likely refers to a tune name or liturgical instruction, possibly echoing Moses' intercessory plea in Deuteronomy 9:26. English renders it 'Do not destroy,' Spanish 'no destruyas,' and French 'ne détruis pas' — all preserving the urgent prohibitive force of the Hebrew jussive.

senses.1: The Hifil jussive (negated) form אַל־תַּשְׁחֵת ('do not destroy'), from the root שָׁחַת meaning 'to ruin, corrupt, destroy.' All eight occurrences appear in the superscriptions of Psalms 57:1, 58:1, 59:1, and 75:1 (each title counted twice in the verse numbering). This is widely understood as a tune name or liturgical direction, possibly alluding to Moses' intercessory cry 'Do not destroy your people' (Deut 9:26) or to a vintner's song (cf. Isa 65:8). Multilingual renderings — English 'do not destroy,' Spanish 'no destruyas,' French 'ne détruis pas' — preserve the prohibitive imperative sense uniformly.

gloss_terse: Nation, people, tribe — a collective term for ethnic or political groups, used in late biblical Hebrew and Aramaic
gloss_readable: This noun denotes a nation or people-group, appearing primarily in the Aramaic sections of Daniel and Ezra. In Daniel's grand court scenes, heralds summon 'peoples, nations, and languages' (Dan 3:4, 7; 5:19; 6:25; 7:14), while Ezra 4:10 lists deported nations. Psalm 117:1 provides the lone Hebrew occurrence, calling all nations to praise the LORD. English 'nation,' Spanish 'nación,' and French 'nations' consistently render the collective sense, while the formulaic Aramaic triplet in Daniel underscores imperial universality.

senses.1: The feminine noun אֻמָּה meaning 'nation, people, tribe,' used in late biblical Hebrew (Ps 117:1) and especially in biblical Aramaic (Daniel and Ezra). In Daniel it appears in the stereotyped court formula 'peoples, nations, and languages' (אֻמַּיָּא, Dan 3:4, 7, 29; 4:1; 5:19; 6:26; 7:14), emphasizing the universal reach of royal decrees and divine sovereignty. Ezra 4:10 uses it of ethnic groups deported by Assyria. The multilingual evidence — English 'nation/nations,' Spanish 'nación/naciones,' French 'nations' — confirms a straightforward collective-ethnic sense with no significant polysemy.

gloss_terse: Four — the cardinal number, used for counting and in compound numerals
gloss_readable: The cardinal number four (אַרְבַּע / אַרְבְּעָה in masculine form) is one of the most common numerals in Scripture. In the Daniel and Ezra passages where this lemma clusters, it counts beasts in apocalyptic vision (Dan 7:2, 3, 6, 17), men walking in the fiery furnace (Dan 3:25), and sacrificial animals (Ezra 6:17, 'four hundred'). Every translation tradition renders it with the simple numeral — English 'four,' Spanish 'cuatro,' French 'quatre' — confirming its purely quantitative, unambiguous function.

senses.1: The cardinal number four (אַרְבַּע feminine, אַרְבְּעָה masculine), used throughout the Hebrew Bible for straightforward enumeration. In Daniel it counts the winds of heaven (7:2), great beasts (7:3), wings and heads of the leopard-beast (7:6), and the four kingdoms (7:17), as well as the four men seen in Nebuchadnezzar's furnace (3:25). In Ezra 6:17 it forms part of the compound 'four hundred' for sacrificial he-goats. Multilingual renderings are uniformly numeric — English 'four,' Spanish 'cuatro,' French 'quatre,' German 'vier' — with zero semantic variation.
